5734.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kléwos (whence Mycenaean Greek 𐀐𐀩𐀺 (ke-re-wo)), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱléwos.

5748.t: From the old oblique stem, *κραν- (*krān-), of κάρη (kắrē, “Homeric form of κάρα (kắrā, “the head”)”) + -ιον (-ĭon, diminutive suffix).

5770.t: Uncertain; possibly from Pre-Greek. Potential cognates include Spanish cuesco (“stone (of fruit)”), though this is rejected by Furnee.

5765.t: Of unclear origin. Traditionally compared with Latin carīna (“ship's keel; shell of a nut”) and Sanskrit करक (karaka, “water jar; coconut (shell)”).

5743.t: From the o-grade κοντ- (kont-) of the root κεντ- (kent-) underlying κεντέω (kentéō, “prick”), κέντρον (kéntron, “centre”). The suffix is -ός (-ós, deverbal adjective and noun suffix).

5774.t: Difficult to trace. The word passed to and from a number of languages (compare Latin cubus (“mass, quantity; cube”)).

5784.t: From λέκος (lékos, “dish; pot; pan”) + -άνη (-ắnē, suffix for utensil names), alleged to be from Pre-Greek; however, see λάγυνος (lắgūnos, “flask”).

5727.t: From κηδεύω (kēdeúō, “to care for”) + -εία (-eíā). The sense of "care for the dead" > "funeral" developed in the Hellenistic Koine era.

5775.t: Perhaps from a Proto-Indo-European *ḱewk- (“white”), with cognates including Sanskrit शोचति (śócati, “to shine, suffer”) and शुक्र (śukrá, “bright, white”), and possibly Old Norse Hǿnir (“god associated with swans and storks”).

5745.t: From Proto-Indo-European *ḱorh₂- (“crow, raven”), apparently of imitative origin and with similar formations across multiple Indo-European branches; see Latin cornīx (“crow”) for more.

5759.t: Probably onomatopoeic. Compare βόμβος (bómbos, “humming, buzzing”), κόναβος (kónabos, “din, clash”) and κόμβα (kómba, “shearwater”).

5771.t: Uncertain; Beekes and Furnee take the word as the usual Pre-Greek, while others have narrowed down the language of origin to possibly Semitic or Hurrian.

5757.t: Unclear. The comparison with Latin curvus (“curved”) presupposes that the Greek adjective continues a reduced grade *kʷr-to-s with u coloring, which is phonetically difficult and places the comparison in doubt.

5773.t: Beekes suggests a Pre-Greek origin due to the presence of variations and rejects a derivation from κυέω (kŭéō); possibly connected to Classical Syriac ܓܘܡܐ (gūmā), Jewish Babylonian Aramaic גוגמא, גגמא (“bean”).

5750.t: Traditionally considered an old verbal noun from κρεμάννυμι (kremánnumi, “to hang”), however Beekes finds this impossible and leaves the etymology unexplained.

5776.t: Etymology tree Proto-Indo-European *ḱewh₁- Proto-Indo-European *-yeti Proto-Indo-European *-éyeti Proto-Indo-European *ḱuh₁éyeti Ancient Greek κύω From Proto-Indo-European *ḱewh₁- (“to swell”).

5764.t: From καρπός (kărpós, “fruit”) + -ιμος (-ĭmos, suffix for adjective of capability).

5783.t: From λείχω (leíkhō, “to lick”), derived with the meaning “the one who licks”, ultimately from Proto-Indo-European *leyǵʰ- (“to lick”).

5719.t: From κατα- (kătă-, “against”) + the root of ἀγορεύω (ăgoreúō, “to speak”).

5711.t: From κατά (katá, “under, down”) + χράομαι (khrắomai, “to use, make use of, take part in, manage, administer”).

5788.t: From a Semitic sound plural of the etymon of λίβανος (lĭ́bănos), which Beekes says derives from a Semitic root cognate to Hebrew לָבָן (“white”) and Arabic لَبَن (laban, “milk”).

5777.t: According to Beekes, probably of Pre-Greek origin. The term has been compared to Georgian [script needed] (kotoxi, “cup”) and Mingrelian [script needed] (koto, “cup”).

5767.t: From Proto-Hellenic *kʰénkʰros, mostly derived from Proto-Indo-European *gʰer-gʰ-r-o- (“pulverized”), reduplicated from the root *gʰer- (“to rub, grind”) with dissimilation r…r > n…r, and further connected with Ancient Greek χερμάς (khermás), χεράς…

5763.t: Beekes finds improbable a derivation from κάπη (kápē, “crib, manger”). Probably related to Latin caupō (“innkeeper”); as the Greek could be from Pre-Greek, this would render the Latin a substrate borrowing, as well.

5798.t: Probably of onomatopoeic origin but compare Armenian լոր (lor, “quail”).

5729.t: The formation is like κνημίς (knēmī́s, “greave”). A comparable meaning can be found in Latin calidus (“with a bless on the head”).

5778.t: Back-formation from κυρόω (kuróō), from Proto-Indo-European *ḱewh₁- (“to swell, be strong”), the same root as κυέω (kuéō, “to be pregnant”), κῦμα (kûma, “wave”), Sanskrit शव॑स् (śávas, “strength, power”) and Irish curadh (“hero”).

5797.t: An onomatopoeic word. In other Indo-European languages we find Albanian lap (“to slurp”), Proto-Slavic *lopati (“to eat greedily”), Lithuanian lapènti (“to absorb greedily”), Old English lapian (“to lap”).
